title: Digestion & Absorption of CHO & Glycolysis
objectives: Understand carbohydrate digestion and absorption processes
Explain the ten enzymatic steps of glycolysis with detailed biochemical transformations
Describe the regulation of glycolysis under varying physiological conditions
Identify clinical disorders related to digestive enzyme deficiencies and glycolytic defects

digestion.title: Carbohydrate Digestion
digestion.content:
Digestion of Carbohydrates

Carbohydrate digestion occurs primarily in the mouth and small intestine, breaking down complex carbohydrates into absorbable monosaccharides.

Key Sites of Digestion

Mouth

Enzyme: Salivary α-amylase (pH 6.6)

Action: Hydrolyzes α(1→4) glycosidic bonds in starch/glycogen

Limitation: Cannot break α(1→6) bonds (branches)

Small Intestine

Enzymes: Pancreatic α-amylase (pH 7.8-8.0) and disaccharidases

Action: Completes digestion to monosaccharides

Disaccharidases

  • Maltase: cleaves maltose → 2 glucose
  • Isomaltase: cleaves isomaltose → glucose
  • Sucrase: cleaves sucrose → glucose + fructose
  • Lactase: cleaves lactose → glucose + galactose
  • Trehalase: cleaves trehalose → glucose

absorption.title: Absorption Mechanisms
absorption.content:
Absorption of Carbohydrates

Occurs primarily in duodenum and upper jejunum via specific transporters:

Transport Mechanisms

Glucose/Galactose: Active Na+-dependent transport via SGLT-1 (also in kidney)

Fructose: Facilitated diffusion via GLUT-5

Portal Circulation: All monosaccharides exit enterocytes via GLUT-2

Fates of Absorbed Glucose

  • Synthesis of complex polysaccharides
  • Glycogen storage
  • Glycolysis for ATP production
  • Pentose phosphate pathway for NADPH and ribose-5-P

enzyme_deficiency.title: Enzyme Deficiencies
enzyme_deficiency.content:
Digestive Enzyme Deficiencies

General Consequences

Undigested carbohydrates cause:

  • Osmotic diarrhea (water drawn into lumen)
  • Bacterial fermentation → gas (CO2, H2), cramps, flatulence

Diagnosis:

Oral tolerance tests and breath H2 measurements

Congenital Sucrase-Isomaltase Deficiency

Prevalence: 2.02% (autosomal recessive)

Treatment: Sucrose restriction, enzyme replacement

Lactose Intolerance

Prevalence: 70% of adults worldwide

Management: Reduce milk, consume yogurt/green vegetables for calcium

glycolysis.title: Glycolysis Pathway
glycolysis.content:
Glycolysis (EMP Pathway)

Ten-step pathway converting glucose to pyruvate with net production of 2 ATP and 2 NADH. Occurs in cytosol of all cells.

Significance

  • Universal pathway in all organisms
  • Sole ATP source in erythrocytes
  • Provides intermediates for other pathways
  • Essential for brain and renal medulla energy

Two Phases

Energy Investment Phase (5 steps)

Consumes 2 ATP to produce glyceraldehyde 3-P

Pay-off Phase (5 steps)

Produces 4 ATP (net 2), 2 NADH, and 2 pyruvate

glycolysis_steps.title: Glycolysis Reactions
glycolysis_steps.content:
Detailed Glycolysis Steps

1. Hexokinase/Glucokinase

Reaction: Glucose → Glucose-6-P (irreversible)

Isozymes: Hexokinase I-III (all tissues), Glucokinase (liver/pancreas β-cells)

3. PFK-1 (Key Regulatory Step)

Reaction: Fructose-6-P → Fructose-1,6-BP

Regulation: Activated by F2,6-BP, AMP; inhibited by ATP, citrate

6. Glyceraldehyde-3-P Dehydrogenase

Reaction: Produces 1,3-BPG + NADH

Inhibitors: Heavy metals (Hg), arsenate

10. Pyruvate Kinase

Reaction: PEP → Pyruvate + ATP

Isoforms: Liver, muscle, erythrocyte

regulation.title: Regulation
regulation.content:
Glycolysis Regulation

Three Key Regulatory Steps

Hexokinase: Inhibited by G6P (except glucokinase)

PFK-1: Main control point; activated by F2,6-BP (insulin), AMP; inhibited by ATP, citrate

Pyruvate Kinase: Activated by F1,6-BP; inhibited by ATP, acetyl-CoA, alanine

Hormonal Control

Insulin: Induces glucokinase, PFK-2, pyruvate kinase

Glucagon: Inhibits liver glycolysis via PKA phosphorylation

clinical.title: Clinical Notes
clinical.content:
Clinical Correlations

Hemolytic Anemia

Causes:

Aldolase A deficiency or pyruvate kinase deficiency

Muscle PFK-1 Deficiency

Symptoms:

Exercise intolerance, improved with lipid fuels

Arsenic Toxicity

Mechanism:

Forms 1-arseno,3-phosphoglycerate → spontaneous hydrolysis without ATP production

Fluoride Inhibition

Application:

Used in blood collection tubes to inhibit enolase and prevent glycolysis in samples

faqs.title: FAQs
faqs.content:
Frequently Asked Questions

Why does glycolysis produce a net of 2 ATP?
The pathway consumes 2 ATP in the investment phase and produces 4 ATP in the payoff phase, resulting in a net gain of 2 ATP per glucose molecule.
How does 2,3-BPG affect oxygen delivery?
2,3-BPG binds hemoglobin, reducing its oxygen affinity and enhancing oxygen release to tissues.
What happens to pyruvate under anaerobic conditions?
Converted to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase to regenerate NAD+ for continued glycolysis.
